cards.f: Seven components of a balanced diet
cards.b: Carbohydrate, fat, protein, vitamins, minerals, fibre, water.
Macro: large amounts (carbohydrate, fat, protein). Micro: small amounts (vitamins, minerals).
Main energy source, stored as glycogen in muscles and liver.
Growth and repair of muscle and other tissues.
Energy store, insulation, protects organs, carries fat-soluble vitamins.
Makes haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in red blood cells.
Keeps digestion working and prevents constipation.
Carbohydrate and protein about 4 kcal; fat about 9 kcal.
Simple: fast energy (sugar). Complex: slow release (pasta, rice, bread).
Eating extra carbohydrate before endurance events to store more glycogen.
Stored form of carbohydrate in muscles and liver.
Thicker blood, higher heart rate and temperature, cramp, fatigue, poor concentration.
Same concentration as body fluids; replaces water, sugar and salts.
Carbohydrate to refill glycogen and protein to repair muscle, plus fluids.

short.q: Explain why a marathon runner would eat more carbohydrate than a weightlifter.
short.model: Marathons use a lot of energy over a long time, so more glycogen is needed. A weightlifter needs more protein for muscle growth.

short.q: Describe two effects of dehydration on performance.
short.model: Blood becomes thicker so heart rate rises, and body temperature increases causing fatigue and cramp.

short.q: Why is calcium important to a teenage gymnast?
short.model: Calcium builds strong bones and teeth. This reduces the risk of fractures during landings.

short.q: Give one source and one function of protein.
short.model: Sources include meat, fish, eggs and beans. It repairs and builds muscle tissue.

short.q: What should an athlete eat in the 2–4 hours before an event, and why?
short.model: A meal high in complex carbohydrate and low in fat and fibre. It releases energy slowly and is easy to digest.
